strengths: Timely and relevant problem: memory- and sample-efficient variants of the Muon optimizer for matrix-structured parameters are of practical interest, and the paper positions itself well against recent theory (Muon, Muon++, SCG, GGNC, SUMO) in a clear comparison table.

The algorithmic combination is reasonable: STORM-style momentum-based variance reduction (to avoid the large batch sizes needed in prior analyses) plus randomized SVD compression of the momentum state is a sensible route to both O(ε^-3) SFO complexity with batch size 1 and reduced state memory.

Convergence is analyzed under both standard Lipschitz smoothness and the generalized (L0, L1)-smoothness condition, the latter of which is more realistic for LLM training; the appendix proofs are detailed and largely follow verifiable standard steps (STORM recursion + randomized SVD error bound of Halko et al.).
The paper is honest that absolute perplexity numbers do not reach state of the art, and reports memory usage alongside accuracy/perplexity.
weaknesses: Assumption 5 (Eq. 10) is very strong and essentially assumes away the hard part for the memory-efficient Option #2: it requires the tail singular values of the momentum matrix to be bounded by ρ‖∇f(W_t)‖_F, i.e., approximate low-rankness of the momentum, with the convergence guarantee only holding when γ = ρ(1 + r̃/(s−1))^{1/2} is small enough (γ ≤ β/(4√r(1−β))). No empirical validation of this low-rank structure (e.g., singular value decay of M_t during training) is provided, so the central claim that the low-memory variant retains O(ε^-3) complexity rests on an unverified and restrictive assumption.

The 'fast' claim is not substantiated: Algorithm 1 requires a full SVD of M_t every iteration (line 4) in addition to the randomized SVD (line 8), which is typically much more expensive than the Newton–Schulz iterations used by practical Muon. No wall-clock runtime, throughput, or step-time comparisons are reported in any experiment, and the paper itself concedes that RSVD 'introduces additional computational cost.'

Experiments are far too small to support claims about 'large models': DistilGPT2 (82M) trained for only 5000 iterations with batch size 8 on a single consumer GPU, and a 22M-parameter ViT on Tiny-ImageNet. No results at any modern LLM scale, no ablations over r̃ and s, no error bars or seeds, and no evidence that the memory savings matter at scale.

Experimental reporting has correctness and rigor issues: Figure 3 (captioned ViT/Tiny-ImageNet) appears inside the DistilGPT2 section and duplicates Figure 4; the text states the learning rate is 0.001 'for all methods' while also claiming each optimizer is 'individually tuned'; the reported gap (LiMuon #1 validation PPL 170 vs. Muon 245 and Muon++ 245) is implausibly large for an optimizer modification of this type and is not explained; momentum β = 0.05 is atypical and unexamined.

Memory savings are modest and incompletely characterized: 7.35→6.30 GB on DistilGPT2 is about 14%, and the table does not break down where savings come from or compare against simpler baselines (e.g., keeping momentum in bf16 or low-rank factorizing the momentum without STORM).

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: repeated typos ('under under', 'we have began', 'a simple at each iteration'), undefined/loose phrasing of Assumption 5, and a duplicated ViT experiment section structure; there is no discussion of limitations, no code release, and insufficient detail (seeds, tuning budgets, hardware memory accounting) for reliable reproduction.

The theory–practice gap is unaddressed: the O(ε^-3) result relies on batch size 1, whereas the experiments use batch size 8+, and the descent analysis assumes exact orthogonalization via full SVD while practical implementations use Newton–Schulz; the paper does not connect its theoretical setting to the regime it experiments in.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: improving the memory and sample complexity of Muon-style optimizers for large-model training.

The idea of combining STORM-style momentum-based variance reduction with randomized SVD to compress the momentum state is a reasonable engineering direction, and the low-rank factorization of momentum (Figure 1) is a simple, deployable memory saving.

Convergence results are provided for four settings (two algorithm variants x Lipschitz and generalized smoothness), and the O(eps^-3) sample complexity with batch size 1 matches the best known rates (e.g., Muon++), with proofs supplied in the appendix.

The generalized smoothness (L0, L1) analysis of a Muon-type iteration is a small but genuine extension of the existing Muon convergence literature, which has mostly assumed standard Lipschitz smoothness.
Experiments cover both a language model (DistilGPT2 on WikiText-103) and a vision model (ViT on Tiny-ImageNet), and report both accuracy/perplexity and peak memory, which is the relevant trade-off.
weaknesses: Limited originality: the method is a fairly mechanical combination of two well-known components (STORM momentum variance reduction from Cutkosky & Orabona 2019 and randomized SVD from Halko et al. 2011) applied to Muon; the analysis adapts standard STORM-style proof techniques rather than introducing a genuinely new analysis framework, despite the claim of a 'totally different' framework.

The central Assumption 5 (a rank-tail bound on the momentum matrix, linking its truncated singular value tail to the gradient norm) is the crux of the Option #2 theory and memory claim, but it is neither derived from any structural property of neural network training nor empirically validated anywhere in the paper. It is unclear whether momentum matrices in real training are approximately low-rank at rank r-hat = 8-10 as used in the experiments.

The algorithm presentation is inconsistent and hard to follow: Algorithm 1 (line 4) performs a full SVD of M_t even under Option #2, which is precisely the memory-constrained variant claiming to store only low-rank factors; it is never clarified how orthogonalization and RSVD interact when only the compressed state is available, nor what the true peak memory footprint is (full gradients and G_t are still m x n transiently).

The empirical evidence only partially supports the headline claims: in the ViT experiments, Muon achieves higher training accuracy (29.69%) than LiMuon(#1) (28.02%), and LiMuon(#2) is beaten by Muon on both training and test accuracy; the advantage over Muon++ (a direct O(eps^-3) competitor) is small and inconsistent across settings. Only the DistilGPT2 perplexity result is clearly favorable.

Experiments are weak on rigor: single runs with no seeds/error bars, no wall-clock or compute-overhead comparison despite RSVD introducing extra cost (the paper itself concedes RSVD 'introduces additional computational cost'), no ablations over the critical hyperparameters (rank r-hat, oversampling s, beta), and very small scale (82M/22M parameters, 5000 iterations) that falls far short of the 'large models' motivation. The final perplexities (142-249 vs. the acknowledged 18.25 state of the art) suggest undertrained baselines, weakening conclusions about relative optimizer quality.

Reproducibility is inadequate: no code release, incomplete hyperparameter specifications (the tuning procedure is described as 'individually tuned for relative optimal performance' without ranges or protocol), and the figures (Figures 2-4) are too small to be legible, making the qualitative convergence claims unverifiable.

There is no limitations discussion and no treatment of the gap between the theoretical assumptions (constant learning rate, rank-tail condition, bounded variance) and the practical setting (cosine schedules, no rank verification).

Numerous presentation defects undermine confidence: repeated typos ('under under', 'Agorithm 2', 'requires a simple at each iteration'), inconsistent notation for singular values (nu vs. sigma), Lemma numbering inconsistencies between the main text and appendix (Lemma 1 vs. Lemma 10, etc.), and blue-highlighted section headings suggesting an unfinished draft.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and active topic: memory- and complexity-efficient variants of the Muon optimizer for matrix-structured parameters of large models.

The combination of STORM-style momentum-based variance reduction with Muon is a natural and reasonable idea, and achieving O(ε^-3) SFO complexity with batch size 1 (avoiding the large b1 = ε^-1 batches required by Muon++) is a genuine, distinguishable contribution.

Providing convergence guarantees under the (L0, L1) generalized smoothness condition, in addition to standard Lipschitz smoothness, is a meaningful relaxation relative to most existing Muon analyses, which rely on strict smoothness.

The paper includes both theory (four theorem settings covering Option #1/#2 under both smoothness assumptions) and experiments (DistilGPT2 and ViT), and the comparison table (Table 1) against Muon, Muon++, SCG, GGNC, and SUMO is helpful for positioning.
The full proofs are provided in the appendix and the main proof steps (e.g., the STORM recursion and the descent lemma with orthogonalized updates) appear largely followable.
weaknesses: The central 'lower memory' claim is not convincingly established by the algorithm as stated. In Algorithm 1, line 4 computes a full SVD of Mt, and Algorithm 2 (RSVD) requires the full matrix A as input, so under Option #2 the full m×n momentum must still be materialized at each iteration; only the *stored* state is compressed. The claimed state memory of (m+n)r̂ in Table 1 applies only to Option #2 under the strong Assumption 5, while Option #1 requires mn memory — the table does not distinguish these cases. The memory claim also needs clarification regarding transient memory and the additional cost of RSVD (relevant since the title claims 'Fast', yet no wall-clock time results are reported).

Assumption 5 is strong and essentially assumes the conclusion for the memory-efficient variant: it requires the tail singular values of the momentum Mt to satisfy (Σ_{j>r̂} ν_j²)^{1/2} ≤ ρ∥∇f(Wt)∥F for all t. This approximate low-rankness of stochastic gradient momentum is neither derived nor empirically validated (e.g., by measuring the effective rank/spectrum of momentum during training), which weakens the significance of the Option #2 theory.

Algorithm 1 is presented inconsistently: lines 7 and 9 both define Mt+1, and line 8 applies RSVD to Mt after Mt+1 has already been computed; the roles of Mt, M̂t, and their indices are confusing and should be rewritten. It is also unclear how the low-rank factors interact with the full SVD at line 4 in Option #2.

The O(ε^-3) results rely on β = O(T^-2/3), i.e., the momentum coefficient must vanish with T, whereas the experiments use fixed βt = 0.05/0.1 — the theory and the practice are disconnected, and this gap is not discussed.

The experimental evidence is thin for a 'large models' claim: DistilGPT2 (82M) with global batch size 8 for 5000 iterations yields perplexities (142–999) far from any meaningful operating point, and ViT (22M) on tiny-ImageNet. There are no wall-clock/throughput comparisons despite 'fast' in the title, no seeds/confidence intervals, and the memory savings are modest (e.g., 7.35→6.30 GB on DistilGPT2). In Table 3, Muon actually attains higher training accuracy than LiMuon(#1). No code is mentioned, hurting reproducibility.

Several presentation problems reduce confidence: repeated typos ('under under', 'Agorithm 2', 'a simple at each iteration', 'Limuon'), the sign of the Zt term is inconsistent between eqs. (18)–(19) and (48)/(53), Lemma 5 is stated imprecisely (independence/zero-mean conditions), Lemma 10 duplicates Lemma 1, and steps such as bounding ∥∇f(Ws)−∇f(Ws−1)∥²F by L²η²r² (vs. L²η²r) are sloppy. Section 5.1 states a single learning rate for all experiments while also claiming per-optimizer tuning.

Novelty is incremental: the algorithm is a fairly direct composition of known components (STORM variance reduction [Cutkosky & Orabona 2019], randomized SVD [Halko et al. 2011], and Muon orthogonalization), and O(ε^-3) SFO complexity for Muon-type methods has already been established by Muon++ (albeit with large batches); the memory contribution hinges on the unvalidated Assumption 5.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant problem: memory- and sample-efficient variants of the Muon optimizer for large-model training.

The proposed algorithm combines two reasonable ideas (STORM-style variance reduction and randomized SVD for low-rank momentum), and Table 1 gives a clear positioning against prior Muon variants (Muon, Muon++, SUMO, etc.).

Convergence guarantees are provided under both (Frobenius/nuclear-norm) Lipschitz and generalized smoothness assumptions, for both exact-SVD and Newton–Schulz variants, including an O(χ_q^3 ε^{-3}) bound for the Newton–Schulz version that improves on the O(χ_q^4 ε^{-4}) of Kim & Oh.
Experiments cover three architectures (Mamba-130M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, ViT) with multiple baselines, per-method hyperparameter tuning, search ranges in Appendix C, and runtime/memory measurements.
weaknesses: Technical soundness issue in the low-rank analysis: Lemma A.4 claims a deterministic, per-iteration error bound ||M̂_t − M_t||_F ≤ γ||M_t||_F for all t, but it is derived from Lemma A.3, which only gives an expected error bound E||A − Â||_F. The expectation is silently dropped, and the proof additionally assumes the spectral tail ratio (∑_{j>r̂}ν_j^2)^{1/2}/||M_t||_F ≤ τ ∈ (0,1) uniformly over t. This bounded spectral decay of the momentum matrix is a strong, unverified assumption on which the entire Option #2 analysis rests; it is not stated as an assumption and does not generally hold for LLM training.

Algorithm/memory inconsistency: with Option #2, the state is stored only as (Û_t, Ŝ_t, V̂_t), yet line 4 of Algorithm 1 requires the SVD of the full matrix M_t (not M̂_t), which cannot be computed without materializing an m×n matrix (or paying reconstruction cost). The claimed state-memory reduction is therefore not clearly supported by the algorithm as written, and the additional RSVD cost per iteration is not quantified.

The headline O(ε^{-3}) comparison in Table 1 is misleading: the O(ε^{-3}) memory-efficient guarantee holds only under the (implicit) spectral-decay assumption, whereas the competing entries' guarantees hold unconditionally; the table does not reflect this qualification.

Novelty is modest: Muon++ already applies momentum-based variance reduction to Muon, and randomized SVD is a standard tool; the main contribution is a combination plus proof adaptation, so the significance rests on the correctness and practical value of the combination, both of which have the issues above.

Experiments are at modest scale and duration (130M–0.5B parameters, 2,000–5,000 iterations), which weakens claims about 'large models.' Also, the memory advantage is marginal in practice (e.g., rank=16 LiMuon uses more memory than Muon on Mamba), so the simultaneous 'lower memory + lower complexity' claim is only partially supported empirically.

Several writing/derivation sloppinesses undermine confidence in the proofs: sign inconsistencies between Eq. (13) and Eq. (17) in the expansion of ζ_t, an unverifiable reference (Kim & Oh, 2026, arXiv:2601.19156) on which the central Newton–Schulz comparison depends, and repeated minor errors (e.g., 'Assumption 4.5 is a natural extension of l2-norm smoothness', stray parentheses in Eqs. (111), (124)).

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and the multi-iteration Newton–Schulz (q=10) plus RSVD inside every step raises wall-clock questions that only one small runtime table (ViT) addresses; the target-loss runtime analysis is not reported for the LLM experiments.

The limitations section is essentially absent; the paper makes multiple 'first study' claims without a discussion of when the low-rank momentum assumption may fail or of the extra RSVD computational overhead.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and practically motivated: combining a STORM-style momentum-based variance-reduced estimator with randomized SVD to reduce the state memory of Muon-type optimizers, and Table 1 clearly situates LiMuon relative to Muon++, SUMO, and exact-SVD analyses.

The convergence analysis is reasonably complete: eight theorem/lemma chains covering exact SVD and Newton–Schulz variants under both Lipschitz and generalized (L0, L1) smoothness, with detailed proofs supplied in the appendix.

The claimed O(ε^-3) complexity with (m+n)r̂ memory, including under Newton–Schulz approximation, is a genuinely improved operating point on the complexity–memory frontier compared to prior variance-reduced Muon (Muon++, mn memory) and SUMO (which needs an additional boundedness assumption).

Experiments cover three architectures (Mamba-130M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, ViT), report memory alongside quality metrics and wall-clock time (Table 5), and the appendix provides full hyperparameter tables and search ranges, which helps reproducibility.
The paper is upfront that Option #1 does not reduce memory and that RSVD adds computational cost, which is honest about the trade-off.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantee for the memory-reduced variant (Option #2) rests on a hidden and strong assumption: Lemma A.4 requires the tail spectrum of every momentum matrix to satisfy a relative decay bound with τ ∈ (0, 1). This low-rank property of Muon momenta is never verified empirically (e.g., no singular-value spectra of momenta during training), and it is not stated as a formal assumption of the problem, so the headline O(ε^-3) + low-memory claim is conditioned on an unvalidated premise.

The contribution is largely a combination of existing components (Muon, STORM variance reduction, Halko-style randomized SVD). The novelty relative to Muon++ is essentially (i) removing gradient clipping and (ii) storing momentum factors at rank r̂; no deeper algorithmic insight or analysis of the interaction between the low-rank approximation and orthogonalization is provided beyond carrying an additive γ-error term through standard STORM proof steps.

Experimental fairness is questionable. LiMuon is run with momentum β = 0.05 while Muon/Muon++/SUMO use 0.95, and weight decay for LiMuon rank variants differs within the same table (e.g., ViT: 0.05 for rank 4/8, 0.01 for rank 16/full), suggesting inconsistent tuning effort across methods. Without an apples-to-apples ablation, the large perplexity gaps (e.g., 47.08 vs. 62.49 for full-rank LiMuon vs. Muon on Mamba) are hard to attribute to the method rather than tuning.

The experiments do not clearly separate the contribution of variance reduction from that of low-rank compression: there is no ablation isolating STORM-only vs. RSVD-only vs. both, and no measurement of the actual rank spectra or approximation error γ of the momentum matrices, which is exactly the assumption the theory needs.

The title's 'Large Models' framing overreaches: the largest model trained is 0.5B for only 2,000 iterations, Mamba-130M for 5,000 iterations. Notably, full-rank LiMuon uses slightly more memory than Muon (22.80 GB vs. 22.20 GB, Table 2), and only ViT includes runtime analysis; no throughput/wall-clock results are reported for the LLM runs, where the extra RSVD overhead could matter.

Writing quality is below the bar: repeated 'first study' claims (at least five times on page 2), typos such as '2((W0) − F∗)' (missing F), 'Without loss of generalization', grammatical errors in Definitions 4.1/4.2 ('If W∗ be...'), and an Algorithm 1/3 presentation where the interplay between the full SVD at line 4 and the factorized storage at line 8 is confusing, particularly which quantities are actually stored per iteration in Option #2.

The β = O(T^{-2/3}) schedule required by the theory is not used in any experiment (constant β), and the practical momentum (0.05) differs by an order of magnitude from the baselines', weakening the theory–practice connection the paper explicitly claims to narrow.
No limitations section and no code release are mentioned, limiting reproducibility of the empirical claims despite the hyperparameter tables.

strengths: The paper makes a sensible and well-motivated combination of three established techniques (Muon-style orthogonalized momentum updates, STORM-style momentum-based variance reduction, and randomized SVD) to target the two recognized weaknesses of Muon variants: sample complexity and state memory.

The theoretical contribution is substantive: convergence guarantees for variance-reduced Muon with O(ε^-3) SFO complexity under both Lipschitz and generalized (L0, L1)-smoothness, for both exact SVD and Newton-Schulz orthogonalization, with the low-rank (Option #2) case analyzed separately (Theorems 4.7–4.23). Full proofs are provided in the appendix and, on inspection, the main steps (momentum error recursion, telescope via ⟨M_t, U_tV_t^T⟩ = ∥M_t∥*, handling of the polar approximation error ε_q) are coherent.

Table 1 provides a clear and honest comparison against prior Muon analyses (Muon, Muon++, SUMO, SCG, Gluon, Kim & Oh), and the paper is transparent that SUMO requires an additional boundedness assumption.

Experiments cover three architectures (Mamba-130M, Qwen2.5-0.5B, ViT), include the relevant recent baselines (Muon, Muon++, SUMO, Lion, AdamW), report both memory and wall-clock time-to-target, and hyperparameters/search ranges are documented in Appendix C, which supports reproducibility.
The relative improvement O(χ_q^3 ε^-3) vs. O(χ_q^4 ε^-4) over Muon with Newton-Schulz (Kim & Oh) is a clean, checkable theoretical claim.
weaknesses: The central memory-saving argument rests on an implicit and unstated assumption. Lemma A.4 assumes (∑_{j>r̂} ν_j²)^{1/2} ≤ τ(∑_j ν_j²)^{1/2} with τ ∈ (0,1), i.e., that the momentum matrix M_t is approximately low-rank with effective rank below r̂. This is a property of the iterates, not guaranteed by any stated assumption, and is exactly the kind of extra condition the authors criticize in SUMO. If τ is close to 1, γ may violate the required constraint γ ≤ β/(3√r(1-β)) and the memory-saving theorem becomes vacuous. The paper should state the spectral-decay requirement as an explicit assumption.

The practical memory gains are marginal: on Mamba-130M, LiMuon(rank=16) uses 22.31 GB vs. 22.80 GB for full rank (~2%), and rank=8 saves only ~11% (Table 2). Meanwhile low-rank variants are slower per step than Muon (25–27 ms vs. 23 ms, Table 5), so the 'light and fast' framing in the title is only weakly supported by the paper's own measurements.

The empirical results for the memory-saving variants are mixed: at r̂=4, LiMuon is clearly worse than Muon++ on Mamba (val. ppl 79.12 vs 56.79) and worse than Muon on Qwen (92.06 vs 67.60); the headline wins come from the full-rank variant, which does not deliver the claimed memory reduction. There are also unexplained inconsistencies (e.g., Muon++ substantially underperforming plain Muon on ViT, Table 4).

Experiments are small-scale and short (130M–0.5B parameters, 2,000–10,000 iterations), which limits the evidence that these gains hold for the 'large models' the title and abstract target. Sample-complexity theory assumes batch size 1 while experiments use batches of 16–128, so the theory-practice gap is not closed.

Novelty is incremental: Muon++ already applies STORM to Muon, and SUMO already targets memory; the genuinely new ingredient is the RSVD-compressed momentum, whose analysis depends on the questionable Lemma A.4 assumption above. Several 'first study' claims are overstated in this light.
The comparison baseline for the Newton-Schulz result (Kim & Oh, 2026) is an arXiv preprint, and the improvement is a constant-factor (χ_q^4 → χ_q^3) rather than an order improvement.

The practical algorithm (Nesterov momentum, fixed 10 Newton-Schulz steps, constant β, weight decay) differs from the analyzed algorithm (constant β, no Nesterov, no weight decay), so the theory does not strictly cover what is evaluated.
